citation.title: The Negative Consequences of Informing Voters about Deepfakes: Evidence from Two Survey Experiments
citation.venue: Journal of Online Trust and Safety

standing_assumptions:
The article is an empirical report of two survey experiments. It contains no theorem, no displayed formula and no formal model; it states no potential-outcome notation and no identification assumption. The setting, as printed (read from the page images; in the article and in the online Appendix the printed page number equals the PDF page number):
Study 1 design (article p. 4): “We randomized participants to receive either the real video or the deepfake version and either information about deepfakes or no additional information in a 2x2 fully factorialized experiment. The four conditions are summarized in Table 1 on the next page.” Table 1 (article p. 5), “Description of Study 1 treatment arms”: rows Real Video (N=696) and Deepfake Video (N=700); columns No Information (N=696) and Information about Deepfakes (N=700); cells (1) N=347, (2) N=349, (3) N=349, (4) N=351.
Study 1 attrition and bounds (article p. 5): “We found that survey attrition varied significantly across treatment conditions (Pearson $\chi^2$(3) = 11.3, p = 0.01): 4.9% of participants in the No Information + Real Video condition did not finish the survey, compared to 1.8% in the three remaining conditions combined. Because our pre-analysis plan did not explicitly stipulate how we would address differential attrition, we used Manski-type worst-case bounds (Manski 2003), which require only that the support of the outcome is bounded when constructing our confidence intervals. These bounds are considered the gold-standard approach when analyzing experiments with attrition (Gerber and Green 2012). Additional details are provided in Section 2 of the Appendix.” Footnote 11 (article p. 5): “The “best” and “worst” cases used to estimate the confidence interval are also covariate adjusted and use robust standard errors.”
Study 1 bounds, method (Appendix p. 5, Section 2, Study 1): “The major deviation is the use of Manski bounds for confidence intervals and statistical significance. For convenience, we provide a brief summary of the method here (for more details, please refer to Manski (2003)). We impose the distribution of outcomes that least favors our hypothesis onto all missing outcomes (i.e., the survey instrument maximum for all missing outcomes in the control and the survey instrument minimum for all missing outcomes in treatment), run a covariate-adjusted OLS regression with robust standard errors over all outcomes, and use the lower bound of the resulting 95% confidence interval as the lower bound of our reported 95% CI. We do the same with a best-case distribution of missing outcomes to estimate the upper bound of our reported 95% CI.”
Study 2 design (article p. 6): “The design of this study was nearly identical to that of Study 1 with the following two modifications. First, Study 2 had only two conditions, Information about Deepfakes and No Information (see Table 2 on the next page), as we did not create a deepfake of Mitt Romney given ethical considerations. Second, our analysis was restricted to participants who knew Romney was a Republican pre-treatment, as Romney’s (formerly) pro-choice position would not appear surprising to participants with no knowledge of his party affiliation. In Study 2, we found no evidence of differential attrition: survey completion rates did not differ significantly across treatment arms.” Table 2 (article p. 7), “Description of Study 2 treatment arms”: Real Video (N=1,925); No Information (N=966); Information about Deepfakes (N=959). Appendix p. 5, Section 2, Study 2: “There were no deviations from the PAP in Study 2.”
Primary outcome (article pp. 6-7): “The primary outcome measure used asked participants the extent to which they agreed with the statement “This video was doctored, manipulated and/or faked by a computer (i.e. it is a ‘Deep Fake’)” on a 7-point agree/disagree scale ranging from strongly disagree (-3) to strongly agree (3).”
Study 2 analysis as planned (amended Study 2 pre-analysis plan, staged as code/pap/DF_Study2_PAP_Amended.pdf, PDF p. 5 of 6, pages unnumbered, Section 6 “Analysis”): “The main analysis will use a covariate adjusted OLS regression. The covariates are: Lucid demographic variables, policy stances, ideology, Big Five personality traits, political knowledge, and political interest.”
Scope of the targets. None of the headline claims P034-H1 to P034-H7 is a mathematical statement (each is an empirical estimate or an interpretive conclusion), so there is no headline target. No finding is rated above Minor (15 confirmed errors, all Minor), so there is no result_touched_by_finding target. The targets below exist because three confirmed Minor errors have mathematical content: P034-E017 (an invalid inference from equal completion rates to random missingness, with an exact counterexample), P034-A001 (coefficients of an interaction model printed under labels that read as overall effects; the contrast algebra) and P034-N010 (two misrounded percentages). The other confirmed errors are not targets because their corrections change no mathematical statement: P034-E003 (which of two computed p-values is printed for the Study 1 deepfake arm; the corrected value, p about 0.003 under the unfavourable completion, is a recalculation from the raw data, and the printed p<0.001 is correct for the complete-case regression); P034-E005, P034-E006, P034-E007, P034-E009, P034-E011 and P034-E019 (defects of code, hand coding and cached output); P034-E012, P034-E015 and P034-E018 (misprints in labels, cross-references, spelling and references, among them “p<.0369” for p = .0369 in the note to Table OA2); P034-N001 and P034-N002 (citations).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Amended Study 2 pre-analysis plan, Section 8 (Missing Data): the rule “If there is no differential attrition, we conclude that missingness occurs at random”, repeated as a justification in the notes to Appendix Figures OA2a and OA3. The witness is the validator's construction and is not in the paper.
canonical_claim.location: Amended Study 2 pre-analysis plan (staged as code/pap/DF_Study2_PAP_Amended.pdf), PDF p. 5 of 6 (pages unnumbered), Section 8, second paragraph, ending on PDF p. 6; online Appendix p. 9 (PDF p. 9), note to Figure OA2a, and p. 18 (PDF p. 18), note to Figure OA3; related sentence in the article, p. 6 (PDF p. 6), Section 2.2
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statements] [Amended Study 2 pre-analysis plan, Section 8 “Missing Data”, second paragraph, PDF p. 5 of 6, ending on PDF p. 6] “Since there may be individuals who are randomized but do not finish the survey (and thus do not provide outcome responses), we will check for differential attrition using a chi-squared test (see line 13 in the Stata code). If there is no differential attrition, we conclude that missingness occurs at random and exclude all affected observations from analysis. If there is differential attrition (i.e., chi-squared p-value<.05), we will use inverse probability weights to weight the population of all subjects who passed the attention checks. The missingness propensity score will be fit via a logistic regression of missingness on covariates, treatment, and their interactions. Any propensity scores under .05 will be Winsorized to 0.05.” [Appendix p. 9, note to Figure OA2a] “The rightmost treatment effect graph uses covariate-adjusted standard errors from an OLS regression, as there was no differential attrition.” [Appendix p. 18, note to Figure OA3] “The confidence intervals in Study 2 are estimated using covariate-adjusted standard errors from an OLS regression, as there was no differential attrition.”
[Counterexample to the implication “no differential attrition, therefore missingness occurs at random”, read as licensing the complete-case covariate-adjusted OLS coefficient as the treatment effect in the randomized population. The construction is the validator's and is not in the paper.] Let $a=37/50$ and $b=13/50$. Let $\Omega=\{0,1\}^5$ with points $\omega=(u,r_0,r_1,x,t)$ and point masses $$P(u,r_0,r_1,x,t)=\tfrac18\;p_0(u)^{r_0}\,(1-p_0(u))^{1-r_0}\;p_1(u)^{r_1}\,(1-p_1(u))^{1-r_1},$$ where $p_0(0)=a$, $p_0(1)=b$, $p_1(0)=b$, $p_1(1)=a$. On $\Omega$ define the potential outcomes $Y(0)=Y(1)=u$, the potential completion indicators $R(0)=r_0$ and $R(1)=r_1$, the pretreatment covariate $X=x$, the treatment $T=t$, the outcome $Y=Y(T)$ and the completion indicator $R=R(T)$; $Y$ is observed if and only if $R=1$. Claims. (i) $P$ is a probability measure on $\Omega$ and all 32 point masses are strictly positive. (ii) Randomization holds: $T$ is independent of $(Y(0),Y(1),R(0),R(1),X)$, and $P(T=1)=1/2$. (iii) The treatment effect is zero for every unit: $Y(1)-Y(0)=0$ on $\Omega$, so $\tau:=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=0$. (iv) There is no differential attrition, exactly: $P(R=1\mid T=0)=P(R=1\mid T=1)=1/2$. (v) Missingness depends on the outcome within treatment arm and covariate stratum: for each $x\in\{0,1\}$, $P(R=1\mid T=0,X=x,Y=0)=37/50$ and $P(R=1\mid T=0,X=x,Y=1)=13/50$, while $P(R=1\mid T=1,X=x,Y=0)=13/50$ and $P(R=1\mid T=1,X=x,Y=1)=37/50$. In particular $R$ is not independent of $Y$ given $(T,X)$, and $R(0)$ is not independent of $Y(0)$. (vi) Complete-case means: $E[Y\mid T=0,R=1]=13/50$ and $E[Y\mid T=1,R=1]=37/50$, so the complete-case difference in means is $12/25\neq 0=\tau$. (vii) Complete-case covariate-adjusted OLS: with $Z=(1,T,X)'$, $$G:=E[ZZ'\mid R=1]=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2&1/2\\ 1/2&1/2&1/4\\ 1/2&1/4&1/2\end{pmatrix},\qquad h:=E[ZY\mid R=1]=\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\ 37/100\\ 1/4\end{pmatrix},$$ $\det G=1/16$, and the unique solution of $G\beta=h$ is $\beta=(13/50,\ 12/25,\ 0)'$. The coefficient on $T$ is $12/25$, not $0$. (viii) A sample in which the plan's test does not reject. Consider the data set of $N=400$ units in which, for each $(t,x)\in\{0,1\}^2$, 50 units have $(T,X)=(t,x)$ and $R=0$ (outcome missing) and 50 units have $(T,X)=(t,x)$ and $R=1$; among the latter, $Y=1$ for 13 units and $Y=0$ for 37 units when $t=0$, and $Y=1$ for 37 units and $Y=0$ for 13 units when $t=1$. Every observed cell of this data set has positive probability under $P$. The $T$-by-$R$ table of counts is $\begin{pmatrix}100&100\\ 100&100\end{pmatrix}$, each expected count $E_{ij}=(\text{row}_i\times\text{column}_j)/N$ equals $100$, and Pearson's statistic $\sum_{i,j}(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2/E_{ij}$ equals $0$, so its $\chi^2_1$ p-value is $1$ and the test does not reject at level $.05$. The least-squares regression of $Y$ on $(1,T,X)$ over the 200 units with $R=1$ has coefficient vector $(13/50,\ 12/25,\ 0)$. (ix) Observational equivalence with a completely-at-random mechanism. Let $\Omega_B=\{0,1\}^6$ with points $(y_0,y_1,r_0,r_1,x,t)$ whose six coordinates are independent under $P_B$ with $P_B(y_0=1)=13/50$, $P_B(y_1=1)=37/50$ and $P_B(r_0=1)=P_B(r_1=1)=P_B(x=1)=P_B(t=1)=1/2$, and define $Y(0)=y_0$, $Y(1)=y_1$, $R(0)=r_0$, $R(1)=r_1$, $X=x$, $T=t$, $Y=Y(T)$, $R=R(T)$. Under $P_B$, $(R(0),R(1))$ is independent of $(Y(0),Y(1),X,T)$ and $E_B[Y(1)-Y(0)]=12/25$. The observed-data laws under $P$ and $P_B$ coincide: for all $t,x\in\{0,1\}$, the probability of $\{T=t,X=x,R=0\}$ is $1/8$ under both; the probability of $\{T=0,X=x,R=1,Y=1\}$ is $13/400$ and that of $\{T=0,X=x,R=1,Y=0\}$ is $37/400$ under both; the probability of $\{T=1,X=x,R=1,Y=1\}$ is $37/400$ and that of $\{T=1,X=x,R=1,Y=0\}$ is $13/400$ under both. Hence the law of the observed data, and in particular any test of completion rates, cannot distinguish the outcome-dependent mechanism with $\tau=0$ from the completely-at-random mechanism with effect $12/25$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The plan and the article define none of these objects formally. From the paper: “differential attrition” is a difference in survey completion rates across treatment arms (article p. 6: “we found no evidence of differential attrition: survey completion rates did not differ significantly across treatment arms”); the check is “a chi-squared test” of completion by arm, the branch for differential attrition being “chi-squared p-value<.05” (plan, Section 8, PDF p. 5); the analysis is “a covariate adjusted OLS regression” (plan, Section 6, PDF p. 5) on the observations that remain after “exclud[ing] all affected observations”. The released code carries out this rule (3-analysis_FINAL.do, lines 32-35: `gen complete2=deepfake!=.`, `tab complete2 treat, col chi`, the comment `/* attrition not differential, so as per PAP we drop missings */`, `drop if complete2==0`). “Missingness occurs at random” is not defined in the plan. Supplied by the validator (derivation.md, sections 2-6), not by the paper: the treatment indicator $T\in\{0,1\}$; potential outcomes $Y(0),Y(1)$; potential completion indicators $R(0),R(1)\in\{0,1\}$; a pretreatment covariate $X$; $Y=Y(T)$, $R=R(T)$; the target $\tau=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]$; randomization as independence of $T$ from $(Y(0),Y(1),R(0),R(1),X)$; the complete-case contrast $E[Y\mid T=1,R=1]-E[Y\mid T=0,R=1]$; the complete-case OLS coefficient as the solution of the normal equations $E[ZZ'\mid R=1]\beta=E[ZY\mid R=1]$ with $Z=(1,T,X)'$; Pearson's statistic for a two-way table of counts $O_{ij}$ with total $N$, $\sum_{i,j}(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2/E_{ij}$ with $E_{ij}=(\sum_j O_{ij})(\sum_i O_{ij})/N$.
canonical_claim.note: The witness is to the plan's rule and to the “as there was no differential attrition” justification in the two Appendix notes; the article's own sentence on p. 6 (“no evidence of differential attrition”) reports a test result and is not refuted. The finding is rated Minor: no bias in the reported Study 2 or pooled estimates is shown (the Study 2 data were not staged), only that the stated justification does not follow. Readings of “missingness occurs at random”: under the readings that would license the complete-case analysis (completion independent of the outcome given treatment and covariates, or completion independent of potential outcomes and covariates within each arm) the conclusion is false in the witness by (v); under the narrowest reading (completion independent of treatment) the conclusion holds in the witness but does not give the complete-case analysis its target, by (vi)-(vii). Parts (i)-(vii) are the core; (viii) shows that the test's non-rejection is a possible outcome of the same process, and (ix) is the validator's stronger check. The validator gives a second instance with 1.2% attrition in each arm, which may be formalized in the same way but is not required: $a=499/500$, $b=489/500$, completion rate $247/250$ in both arms, complete-case means $489/988$ and $499/988$, OLS coefficients $(489/988,\ 5/494,\ 0)$, $\tau=0$. Neither instance describes the actual survey data. All values were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic when these targets were fixed and agree with the validator's exact-output.txt. Also touches headline claims P034-H4 and P034-H5, which use the same Study 2 complete-case sample.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Amended Study 2 pre-analysis plan, Section 8 (Missing Data), second paragraph, as repaired by Sol; the same repair applies to the clause “as there was no differential attrition” in the notes to Appendix Figures OA2a and OA3
canonical_claim.location: Amended Study 2 pre-analysis plan (staged as code/pap/DF_Study2_PAP_Amended.pdf), PDF p. 5 of 6 (pages unnumbered), Section 8; online Appendix p. 9 (PDF p. 9) and p. 18 (PDF p. 18)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed sentence that is replaced: amended Study 2 pre-analysis plan, Section 8, PDF p. 5] “If there is no differential attrition, we conclude that missingness occurs at random and exclude all affected observations from analysis.” [Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P034-E017, prior_correction.corrected_text; the same repair as smallest_repair), verbatim] “If the chi-squared test does not reject, we will report no detected difference in completion rates across treatment arms. This result does not establish random or ignorable outcome missingness. Complete-case covariate-adjusted OLS requires a separate identifying condition; for example, within the target population, completion under each treatment is independent of potential outcomes and pretreatment covariates, with positive completion probability. The test does not verify that condition. If a suitable identifying condition cannot be justified, we will report attrition bounds or sensitivity analyses.”
[Mathematical content of the corrected text, with every hypothesis; notation of P034-T1 and of the validator's derivation.md, sections 2 and 8] [Setting] A probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ carrying a treatment indicator $T\in\{0,1\}$; real potential outcomes $Y(0),Y(1)$ with $E[Y(t)^2]<\infty$; potential completion indicators $R(0),R(1)\in\{0,1\}$; and a vector of pretreatment covariates $X\in\mathbb R^k$ with $E\|X\|^2<\infty$. The realized outcome is $Y=Y(T)$ and the realized completion indicator is $R=R(T)$; $Y$ is observed if and only if $R=1$. The target is $\tau=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]$. [Hypotheses] (H1, randomization) $T$ is independent of $(Y(0),Y(1),R(0),R(1),X)$ and $0<P(T=1)<1$. (H2, the separate identifying condition) for each $t\in\{0,1\}$, $R(t)$ is independent of $(Y(0),Y(1),X)$ and $P(R(t)=1)>0$. [Statement] Under (H1) and (H2): (a) $P(T=t,R=1)=P(T=t)\,P(R(t)=1)>0$ for $t=0,1$, so that conditioning on $\{T=t,R=1\}$ is well defined and $p:=P(T=1\mid R=1)\in(0,1)$. (b) $E[Y\mid T=t,R=1]=E[Y(t)]$ for $t=0,1$; hence the complete-case difference in means is the target, $E[Y\mid T=1,R=1]-E[Y\mid T=0,R=1]=\tau$. (c) For $t=0,1$ the conditional law of $X$ given $\{T=t,R=1\}$ equals the law of $X$; in particular $E[(T-p)X\mid R=1]=0$. (d) Complete-case covariate-adjusted OLS: with $Z=(1,T,X')'$, $G=E[ZZ'\mid R=1]$ and $h=E[ZY\mid R=1]$, every solution $\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_T,\beta_X')'$ of the normal equations $G\beta=h$ has $\beta_T=\tau$; if $G$ is nonsingular the solution is unique. [What the correction removes] (e) (H2) does not follow from (H1) together with equal completion rates $P(R=1\mid T=0)=P(R=1\mid T=1)$: in the model of P034-T1, (H1) holds and both completion rates equal $1/2$, yet (H2) fails, $\tau=0$ and $\beta_T=12/25$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The plan and the article define none of these objects formally. From the paper: “differential attrition” is a difference in survey completion rates across treatment arms (article p. 6: “we found no evidence of differential attrition: survey completion rates did not differ significantly across treatment arms”); the check is “a chi-squared test” of completion by arm, the branch for differential attrition being “chi-squared p-value<.05” (plan, Section 8, PDF p. 5); the analysis is “a covariate adjusted OLS regression” (plan, Section 6, PDF p. 5) on the observations that remain after “exclud[ing] all affected observations”. The released code carries out this rule (3-analysis_FINAL.do, lines 32-35: `gen complete2=deepfake!=.`, `tab complete2 treat, col chi`, the comment `/* attrition not differential, so as per PAP we drop missings */`, `drop if complete2==0`). “Missingness occurs at random” is not defined in the plan. Supplied by the validator (derivation.md, sections 2-6), not by the paper: the treatment indicator $T\in\{0,1\}$; potential outcomes $Y(0),Y(1)$; potential completion indicators $R(0),R(1)\in\{0,1\}$; a pretreatment covariate $X$; $Y=Y(T)$, $R=R(T)$; the target $\tau=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]$; randomization as independence of $T$ from $(Y(0),Y(1),R(0),R(1),X)$; the complete-case contrast $E[Y\mid T=1,R=1]-E[Y\mid T=0,R=1]$; the complete-case OLS coefficient as the solution of the normal equations $E[ZZ'\mid R=1]\beta=E[ZY\mid R=1]$ with $Z=(1,T,X)'$; Pearson's statistic for a two-way table of counts $O_{ij}$ with total $N$, $\sum_{i,j}(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2/E_{ij}$ with $E_{ij}=(\sum_j O_{ij})(\sum_i O_{ij})/N$. For this target the covariate $X$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^k$ and the conditional expectations given $\{R=1\}$ and given $\{T=t,R=1\}$ are ordinary conditional expectations given events of positive probability (part (a)).
canonical_claim.note: (H2) is the explicit sufficient condition the validator gives (derivation.md, section 8: “requiring $R(t)$ to be independent of $(Y(0),Y(1),X)$ for each $t$, with positive completion probability”), which the validator describes as stronger than necessary but explicit and sufficient; it is Sol's “for example” condition written in symbols. The statement is a population identification result: it says nothing about sampling error, robust standard errors or the power of the chi-squared test, and it is not asymptotic. Part (d) follows from (b) and (c) by multiplying the normal equations on the left by $(-p,\ 1,\ 0')$, which gives $p(1-p)\beta_T=E[(T-p)Y\mid R=1]=p(1-p)\tau$. Part (e) is a corollary of P034-T1 and should reuse its definitions. The remaining sentences of the corrected text (report no detected difference; report bounds or sensitivity analyses when no identifying condition can be justified) are reporting instructions and not mathematical statements. The paper's outcomes are bounded survey scales and its covariates are finitely many, so the moment conditions hold in the application; a formalization restricted to finite sample spaces would be a restriction of this statement and should be recorded as such.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Tables OA5 and OA6, first rows (“Information Treatment Effect”, “Deepfake Treatment Effect”), read as effects averaged over the other randomized factor. The witness is the validator's construction and is not in the paper.
canonical_claim.location: Online Appendix p. 13 (PDF p. 13), Table OA5, and p. 14 (PDF p. 14), Table OA6; the article, p. 9 (PDF p. 9), Section 3.1, refers the reader to these Appendix sections
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] [Appendix p. 13] “Table OA5: Study 1 – Information about deepfakes has no impact on favorability, vote choice, or support for essential oils in medicine (but we are underpowered)”. Columns: Favor; Vote; More Essential Oils in Medicine? Rows: Information Treatment Effect: -0.22, -0.10, -0.25; 95% Upper Bound: 0.25, 0.08, 0.26; 95% Lower Bound: -0.73, -0.31, -0.75. [Appendix p. 14] “Table OA6: Study 1 – Deepfakes have no impact on favorability, vote choice, or support for essential oils in medicine (but we are underpowered)”. Same columns. Rows: Deepfake Treatment Effect: 0.19, 0.05, -0.14; 95% Upper Bound: 0.67, 0.24, 0.39; 95% Lower Bound: -0.32, -0.16, -0.63. Note printed under each table: “As mentioned in the PAP, this analysis excludes participants who are likely supporters of alternative medicine. This is defined as ALL participants EXCEPT those who BOTH oppose government mandates for vaccination AND support government subsidies for acupuncture procedures.”
[Counterexample to the identity under which the printed labels would be complete: “in a model containing both treatment indicators and their product, the coefficient on one treatment indicator equals the effect of that treatment averaged over the other treatment”. The construction is the validator's and is not in the paper.] Let $w,v\in\{0,1\}$ and take a 2x2 factorial with cell values $\mu(0,0)=0$, $\mu(1,0)=0$, $\mu(0,1)=0$, $\mu(1,1)=2$. (i) The unique $(a,b,c,d)\in\mathbb R^4$ with $\mu(w,v)=a+bw+cv+dwv$ in all four cells is $(a,b,c,d)=(0,0,0,2)$; equivalently, for the data set of four units, one in each cell, with outcomes $\mu(w,v)$, the least-squares fit of the outcome on $(1,w,v,wv)$ is exact with coefficient vector $(0,0,0,2)$. (ii) The coefficient on $w$ is $b=\mu(1,0)-\mu(0,0)=0$, whereas the effect of $w$ averaged over $v$ with equal weights is $\tfrac12[\mu(1,0)-\mu(0,0)]+\tfrac12[\mu(1,1)-\mu(0,1)]=1$. (iii) The coefficient on $v$ is $c=\mu(0,1)-\mu(0,0)=0$, whereas the effect of $v$ averaged over $w$ with equal weights is $\tfrac12[\mu(0,1)-\mu(0,0)]+\tfrac12[\mu(1,1)-\mu(1,0)]=1$. Hence the coefficient on a treatment indicator in such a model and the effect of that treatment averaged over the other factor are different quantities in general.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The paper prints no model for these tables; the only description is Appendix p. 19 (Section 5, Study 1): “Due to the necessity of using bounds, we were severely underpowered when examining the secondary research questions in Study 1. We assessed whether information about deepfakes or deepfakes themselves have any impact on favorability towards the politician or the extreme policy (mandating doctors to use essential oils to treat cancer). As shown in Section 3, Tables 3-4, we saw no statistically significant differences.” From the released code (4-Supplementary-Materials_FINAL.do, lines 508-585, and manski_ci.ado, lines 30-31): each entry of the first row is `_b[treat]` from `reg outcome treat covars if study==1 & !(acu==1 & pro_vax==0), robust`, with `treat` equal to `tr_warn` (Table OA5) or `tr_deepfake` (Table OA6) and `covars` equal to `pro_vax acupuncture conlib imputed_conlib i.party hhi`, the other treatment indicator and `tr_warn##tr_deepfake`. `tr_warn` is 1 in the information (warning) condition and 0 otherwise; `tr_deepfake` is 1 for the deepfake video and 0 for the real video (1-study1_data_cleanup_FINAL.do, lines 216-229). So the fitted regression function is $m(w,v,z)=a+bw+cv+dwv+\gamma'z$ with $w$ the information indicator, $v$ the deepfake indicator and $z$ the covariates; the first row of Table OA5 is $b$ and the first row of Table OA6 is $c$. The bound rows come from the same coefficient in the worst-case and best-case completions (Appendix p. 5, transcribed in the standing assumptions) and are not part of this target. The contrasts a reader would expect, from the Study 1 pre-analysis plan (staged as code/pap/DF_Study1_PAP_final.pdf, PDF pp. 1-2), do not condition on the other factor: “S_H1a: Are DeepFakes as persuasive as real videos with respect to the favorability/likelihood of voting for the faked politician? Among those who are NOT likely to support the expansion of alternative medicine: [DeepFake] compared to [Real] → Increase in Support”; “S_H1b: Do warnings reduce the persuasive impact of videos with respect to the favorability/likelihood of voting for the faked politician? Among those who are NOT likely to support the expansion of alternative medicine: [Warning] compared to [NoWarning] → Increase in Support”; “S_H2: Are DeepFakes as persuasive as real videos with respect to the position articulated by the fake politician? [DeepFake] compared to [Real] → Decrease in Support for the Expansion of Essential Oils in Medicine”; “S_H3: Do warnings reduce the persuasive impact of videos with respect to the position articulated by the fake politician? [Warning] compared to [NoWarning] → Decrease in Support for the Expansion of Essential Oils in Medicine”.
canonical_claim.note: The printed rows do not assert the identity. The validator records false_as_printed = false: the 18 entries are correct for the contrasts fitted, and the confirmed defect is that the labels “Information Treatment Effect” and “Deepfake Treatment Effect” omit the reference condition (rated an error, Minor, because the intended contrast is not clear from the page). The witness shows why the omission matters: the two readings are different quantities. Part (ii) is the validator's theorem `balanced_counterexample` in check.lean (fitted with $(a,b,c,d,k)=(0,0,0,2,0)$); part (iii) is the same example read for the other factor; the validator's Lean file compiles without sorry and may be reused once checked against this statement. In the actual data the fitted interaction coefficients are about -0.153 (Favor), -0.065 (Vote) and -0.041 (Oils), so for example the printed -0.22 (Favor, Table OA5) is the information effect at the real video while the equal-weight average of the fitted contrasts is about -0.295; those values are recalculations from the raw data, not targets.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Tables OA5 and OA6, titles, first-row labels and notes, as repaired by Sol
canonical_claim.location: Online Appendix p. 13 (PDF p. 13), Table OA5, and p. 14 (PDF p. 14), Table OA6
canonical_claim.statement:
[Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P034-A001, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Tables OA5–OA6 report reference-condition main coefficients from covariate-adjusted models including information, video type, and their interaction. OA5 compares information with no information at real video (deepfake=0); OA6 compares deepfake with real video at no information (warning=0). The displayed attrition intervals include zero. These are not effects averaged across the other treatment factor; reporting such averages would require separately specified contrasts.” [Corrected row labels, from smallest_repair] Table OA5: “Information treatment effect at real video (deepfake=0)”; Table OA6: “Deepfake treatment effect without information (warning=0)”. The 18 printed numbers are unchanged.
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] [Setting] Let $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb R^k$ be arbitrary, and let $m(w,v,z)=a+bw+cv+dwv+\gamma'z$ for $w,v\in\{0,1\}$ and $z\in\mathbb R^k$ be the fitted regression function, where $w$ is the information indicator, $v$ the deepfake indicator and $z$ the covariate vector. Nothing is assumed about the coefficients. [Statement] For every $z\in\mathbb R^k$: (i) $m(1,v,z)-m(0,v,z)=b+dv$ for $v\in\{0,1\}$; in particular the information contrast at the real video is $m(1,0,z)-m(0,0,z)=b$ and at the deepfake video is $m(1,1,z)-m(0,1,z)=b+d$. (ii) $m(w,1,z)-m(w,0,z)=c+dw$ for $w\in\{0,1\}$; in particular the deepfake contrast without information is $m(0,1,z)-m(0,0,z)=c$ and with information is $m(1,1,z)-m(1,0,z)=c+d$. (iii) For every real weight $q$ on $v=1$ (in particular every $q\in[0,1]$), the information contrast averaged over video type is $(1-q)[m(1,0,z)-m(0,0,z)]+q[m(1,1,z)-m(0,1,z)]=b+qd$. (iv) For every real weight $p$ on $w=1$ (in particular every $p\in[0,1]$), the deepfake contrast averaged over information is $(1-p)[m(0,1,z)-m(0,0,z)]+p[m(1,1,z)-m(1,0,z)]=c+pd$. (v) $b+qd=b$ if and only if $qd=0$, and $c+pd=c$ if and only if $pd=0$; so for positive weights the coefficient equals the averaged contrast only when $d=0$. Consequently the first row of Table OA5, the coefficient $b$, is the information effect at the real video, and the first row of Table OA6, the coefficient $c$, is the deepfake effect without information; neither is an effect averaged over the other randomized factor unless the interaction coefficient is zero.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The paper prints no model for these tables; the only description is Appendix p. 19 (Section 5, Study 1): “Due to the necessity of using bounds, we were severely underpowered when examining the secondary research questions in Study 1. We assessed whether information about deepfakes or deepfakes themselves have any impact on favorability towards the politician or the extreme policy (mandating doctors to use essential oils to treat cancer). As shown in Section 3, Tables 3-4, we saw no statistically significant differences.” From the released code (4-Supplementary-Materials_FINAL.do, lines 508-585, and manski_ci.ado, lines 30-31): each entry of the first row is `_b[treat]` from `reg outcome treat covars if study==1 & !(acu==1 & pro_vax==0), robust`, with `treat` equal to `tr_warn` (Table OA5) or `tr_deepfake` (Table OA6) and `covars` equal to `pro_vax acupuncture conlib imputed_conlib i.party hhi`, the other treatment indicator and `tr_warn##tr_deepfake`. `tr_warn` is 1 in the information (warning) condition and 0 otherwise; `tr_deepfake` is 1 for the deepfake video and 0 for the real video (1-study1_data_cleanup_FINAL.do, lines 216-229). So the fitted regression function is $m(w,v,z)=a+bw+cv+dwv+\gamma'z$ with $w$ the information indicator, $v$ the deepfake indicator and $z$ the covariates; the first row of Table OA5 is $b$ and the first row of Table OA6 is $c$. The bound rows come from the same coefficient in the worst-case and best-case completions (Appendix p. 5, transcribed in the standing assumptions) and are not part of this target. The contrasts a reader would expect, from the Study 1 pre-analysis plan (staged as code/pap/DF_Study1_PAP_final.pdf, PDF pp. 1-2), do not condition on the other factor: “S_H1a: Are DeepFakes as persuasive as real videos with respect to the favorability/likelihood of voting for the faked politician? Among those who are NOT likely to support the expansion of alternative medicine: [DeepFake] compared to [Real] → Increase in Support”; “S_H1b: Do warnings reduce the persuasive impact of videos with respect to the favorability/likelihood of voting for the faked politician? Among those who are NOT likely to support the expansion of alternative medicine: [Warning] compared to [NoWarning] → Increase in Support”; “S_H2: Are DeepFakes as persuasive as real videos with respect to the position articulated by the fake politician? [DeepFake] compared to [Real] → Decrease in Support for the Expansion of Essential Oils in Medicine”; “S_H3: Do warnings reduce the persuasive impact of videos with respect to the position articulated by the fake politician? [Warning] compared to [NoWarning] → Decrease in Support for the Expansion of Essential Oils in Medicine”. The printed tables being relabelled are transcribed in P034-T3.
canonical_claim.note: A change of label, not of numbers: the validator reproduces all 18 printed entries from the raw data (agreement with the cached table within 1e-8), and the bound intervals include zero under either contrast. “The displayed attrition intervals include zero” is an empirical statement and is not a target. Parts (i)-(v) are the validator's Lean theorems warning_effect, deepfake_effect, oa5_reference_contrast, oa6_reference_contrast, warning_average, deepfake_average and warning_average_equals_main_iff (check.lean, compiled without sorry; the covariate term there is a scalar $k=\gamma'z$); they may be reused once checked against this statement, and the second equivalence in (v) is the same statement with $(c,p)$ in place of $(b,q)$. The statement is the algebra of the fitted function. That Stata's `tr_warn##tr_deepfake` expands to the two indicators and their product without centring, and that `_b[treat]` is $b$ or $c$, are facts about the released code and not Lean matters.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Table OA3 (Study 2 - Hand-coded Romney facts across conditions), Total column, rows “Subjective Evaluation of Character” and “Stance on Other Policies”, corrected
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed, Appendix p. 11, Table OA3; columns: No Info about Deepfakes | Info about Deepfakes | Total] “Subjective Evaluation of Character (e.g., trusworthy, traitor, etc.)”: 9.2% | 9.3% | 9.3%; N: 266 | 268 | 534. “Stance on Other Policies”: 0.8% | 0.9% | 0.9%; N: 24 | 25 | 49. “Total”: 100% | 100% | 100%; N: 2,898 | 2,877 | 5,775. [Corrected, from Sol's smallest_repair] In the Total column the percentage for Subjective Evaluation of Character is 9.2% (printed 9.3%) and the percentage for Stance on Other Policies is 0.8% (printed 0.9%). [Mathematical content] Each percentage in the table is $100$ times the count in its cell divided by the count at the foot of its column, rounded to one decimal place; a one-decimal number $r$ is the rounding of $x$ when $r-\tfrac1{20}\le x<r+\tfrac1{20}$. (i) $266+268=534$, $24+25=49$ and $2898+2877=5775$. (ii) $100\cdot\frac{534}{5775}=\frac{712}{77}$ and $\frac{915}{100}\le\frac{712}{77}<\frac{925}{100}$, so the rounding is $9.2$; the printed $9.3$ is not the rounding, because $\frac{712}{77}<\frac{925}{100}$. (iii) $100\cdot\frac{49}{5775}=\frac{28}{33}$ and $\frac{75}{100}\le\frac{28}{33}<\frac{85}{100}$, so the rounding is $0.8$; the printed $0.9$ is not the rounding, because $\frac{28}{33}<\frac{85}{100}$. (iv) With these two cells corrected, each of the 39 category percentages of Table OA3 (13 rows by 3 columns, transcribed in definitions_needed) is the rounding of $100\times$ count $/$ column total, each row's Total count is the sum of its two condition counts, and each column of counts sums to the total printed at its foot ($2898$, $2877$, $5775$).

canonical_claim.note: The most marginal target on the list: an arithmetic slip in a descriptive table, included because the author's instruction covers every confirmed error in a mathematical statement at any severity and the corrected cells are exact arithmetic from the printed counts. Counts and every analysis are unaffected (rated Minor). No cell of the table lies at a rounding tie, so the half-up convention in the statement is immaterial: the two printed values also fail the two-sided test $|x-r|\le\tfrac1{20}$, since $9.3-\frac{712}{77}=\frac{41}{770}>\frac1{20}$ and $0.9-\frac{28}{33}=\frac{17}{330}>\frac1{20}$. The printed values are what results from rounding twice ($9.2467\ldots\to 9.25\to 9.3$ and $0.8484\ldots\to 0.85\to 0.9$). Confirmed in batch validation by recalculation; all 39 percentages, the row sums and the column sums were recomputed exactly from the page image when these targets were fixed.
